A new localized ceasefire negotiated by IAEA Director General @rafaelmgrossi took effect this morning to help prevent a nuclear accident in Ukraine during the military conflict. 

The eighth such IAEA-brokered temporary truce will enable repairs of equipment in a 330 kilovolt (kV) switchyard, close to the Zaporizhzhya Thermal Power Plant (ZTPP), that has been damaged by military activity. 

This will in turn strengthen the connection between the nearby Zaporizhzhya Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP) and its sole remaining external power line, the Ferosplavna-1, and reduce the risk of another loss of off-site power. 

The ZNPP’s continued connection to the electrical grid is more important than ever as its fuel reserves for emergency diesel generators have been running low in recent months, weakening this last line of defence against a complete station blackout. 

Following demining, the repair work is expected to last several days, carried out on the frontline of the conflict and monitored by an IAEA team on the ground. 

DG Grossi says the Russian Federation and Ukraine engaged constructively with the IAEA to pave the way for the latest ceasefire, showing that persistent diplomatic efforts can yield concrete results that benefit both sides also in the most difficult and challenging of circumstances. 

The IAEA will continue its indispensable work to ensure nuclear safety and security during the conflict, DG Grossi says.

Today is probably a good time to check in on things with @privy_io, which became part of @stripe just over a year ago.

Our acquisition was predicated on three factors: stablecoin growth, self-custody as a key enabler of broader global coverage, and rapidly increasing demand for programmable financial infrastructure. As we said at the time, "money has to reside somewhere, and Privy builds the world's best programmable vaults."

Since then, the Privy team has executed exceptionally well: assets in Privy wallets have grown ~25x, monthly active developers are up ~3x, revenue is up ~9x, and Privy now facilitates nearly $25B of monthly transaction volume. @tryramp, @Deel, @Klarna, @felixpago, @HyperliquidX, and thousands of other businesses are building embedded banking functionality on Privy.

At Stripe, we're deeply integrating Privy into Treasury, @Link, and Connect. In each case, it's accelerating our global expansion, and enabling us to build better functionality faster. (Coming soon: @Link balances.)

We're also seeing that Privy's wallet infrastructure is the ideal substrate for agents to transact and earn -- live today with @merit_systems, @orthogonal_sh, @Nevermined_ai, @prlnet, and more. Developers prefer programmable financial infrastructure, but agents need it. We expect that the agentic economy will continue to grow extremely quickly.

note_tweet.text:
A long-term perspective on humanity’s battle against malaria.

According to the latest data from the World Health Organization, the global death rate from malaria has almost halved since the year 2000.

The chart above puts this recent progress into a larger historical perspective. It combines the latest estimates from the WHO and the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation with those for the 20th century published by the late malaria researcher Richard Carter. Since 1900, the global death rate has declined by 96%. If it were still as high as it was then, around 16 million people would die from malaria every year instead of 610,000.

Behind this long-run decline is a shift in the distribution of the burden of malaria. In the first half of the 20th century, most malaria victims died in the Asian tropics. It was the substantial progress there — as well as in the Mediterranean and in the Americas — that made this vast improvement in human health possible.

Today, more than 9 out of 10 malaria deaths occur in Africa. This means that the recent progress shown in the chart is, above all, Africa’s progress.

(written by @MaxCRoser)

note_tweet.text:
I'm delighted to share our new paper, "Prioritizing demand-side use of clean hydrogen for cost-effective mitigation," published today in Nature Climate Change.  @NatureClimate 

Clean hydrogen can play a pivotal role in decarbonizing hard-to-abate sectors. However, producing it is energy-intensive and costly, and near-term supply is likely to remain limited. Prioritizing applications that deliver the greatest environmental and economic benefits is therefore essential.

We compare hydrogen technologies with competing low-carbon options across ten US sectors around 2035, assessing both emissions and mitigation costs. Our main findings:

1️⃣ Prioritize high-value uses. Steelmaking, oil refining, and ammonia production emerge as "no-regret" applications, offering substantial emissions reductions at comparatively low mitigation costs.

2️⃣ Consider the alternatives. For road and rail transport, battery electrification delivers lower emissions at lower cost than hydrogen. Cement, firm power generation, methanol production, and long-haul shipping and aviation remain "maybe" applications, with their competitiveness depending on future hydrogen costs and competing technologies.

3️⃣ Making hydrogen cheaper does not automatically direct it to the most valuable uses. Uniform production subsidies can disproportionately benefit hydrogen-intensive applications while providing insufficient support for high-value uses.

These findings highlight the need to pair production support with sector-specific demand-side policies. For steelmaking, demonstration funding, government-backed financing, and public procurement of low-carbon steel can help reduce investment risks and strengthen demand.

I'm very grateful to my co-authors @DeniseMauzerall, @JesseJenkins, Mohamed Atouife, Fangwei Cheng, Qian Luo, and Amarasinghage T.D. Perera for their contributions and collaboration!

Read the full paper here: https://t.co/lGHIhfkmR1

note_tweet.text:
I've been thinking a lot about data bottlenecks, and I'm not sure who else is screaming this from the hilltops. I feel like I'm taking crazy pills looking at the jagged frontier thinking it's smooth if you order by data volume.

the spikes in the jagged frontier are tasks with tons of data (either static or simulated; think math, programming, games), and the valleys are tasks with little or no data (cooking a lasagna, olfaction, manufacturing a passenger train). I don't know of any exceptions. 

if you order the jagged frontier by data it looks like a spiral frontier. models are superintelligent where we have enormous data, and progressively less so as we have less data. some tasks may draw data from static lakes of data, some may be from limitless waterfalls from simulators that convert compute into data. but ultimately, intelligence on a task is proportional to the data absorbed by the model for that task. 

scaling laws are real. if you are not bound by compute or algorithms (increasingly we are not), then intelligence is proportional to data. since we don't have a very good notion of task similarity, it's often difficult to know if data for one task will help you with another, without training a model and seeing. but, it doesn't seem like chess data helps much with math performance and vice versa. so when I refer to data, I refer to data that is task-relevant. 

maybe we call this the 'no shortcuts hypothesis'. all the rules-of-thumb about learning are at the root, the same -- Malcom Gladwell's 10,000 hours, Moravec's Paradox, Scaling Laws, the Bitter Lesson, Age of experience. If your learning system (model, brain, whatever) is unconstrained by compute, intelligence is proportional to accumulated experience. no shortcuts. want to be superhuman at chess? play all the chess, more than the whole species combined (good thing a model can do that in 24 hours). want to be superhuman at math? build a math simulator and lock the model in it and run it faster than reality. superhuman at coding? first, collect all public examples of humans writing and responding to code ever, make the model learn from that first, and then lock the model in a simulator where it fixes bug after bug, faster than realtime.

superhuman at image generation? no shortcuts. but here, we don't have a simulator. so now we're moving around the spiral frontier away from closed-loop into large static lakes. still big enough to be superhuman though, which also applies to video, text, and audio. oh! and once you have a superhuman model, you can use it to bootstrap other tasks by making a superhuman model a judge on other tasks. 

let's keep marching along the spiral frontier, out of the realm of data abundance, simulators and large static lakes. 

biology? no shortcuts. go get a ton of data. and be freaking careful! you can get bad data in biology pretty easily. tilting a well plate 5 degrees the wrong way can ruin an experiment. so make sure you understand the domain, otherwise you're going to have to filter a lot out. 

robotics? no shortcuts. get the data. if you can build a simulator, do it, but be mindful our simulators don't have perfect correspondence with reality. so, build an arm farm. fold 1M shirts, put 1B balls in cups. play ping pong forever. 

olfaction? no shortcuts. smell the world. build a laboratory of chemical sensors, an international network of trained sensory panelists, a scent production factory, and link them all together. make millions of samples. smell millions of samples. take billions of chemical sensor readings. 

I totally buy super intelligence as a concept because I feel it, I use it for coding, the breakthrough math results speak for themselves. I see RSI coming, because how could an all-digital task like ML research and model building not fall to the current paradigm? But the notion that AI will come for everything, all at once, irrespective of domain, feels silly, because there are no shortcuts. if you want a specific form of intelligence, you have to get the data. 

looking at you @willdepue, I feel like we're both seeing the same thing

note_tweet.text:
SpaceX now sells an AI phone agent for $4.80 an hour. Offshore call center agents in the Philippines, the outsourcing capital of the world, bill $8 to $18 an hour fully loaded.

And that comparison actually flatters the humans.

A human agent gets paid for the whole hour. Breaks, coaching, after-call notes, the dead air between one call ending and the next one ringing. Grok bills 8 cents per minute of actual conversation and nothing else.

Run it on a Manila seat. Roughly $1,700 a month fully loaded, with around 110 hours of real talk time once you strip out everything that isn't a customer on the line. That comes to about 26 cents per talking minute, more than 3x the Grok rate.

Cheap only matters if the thing can finish the call, and SpaceX tested this one on its own customers first. Starlink's support line takes about 20,000 calls on a weekday. Roughly 70% of support calls now end without a human ever picking up. One agent verifies who you are, troubleshoots the dish, issues the credit, and ships the replacement hardware.

Calls also don't arrive evenly. Starlink sees about half the volume on weekends and spikes during promos. A human call center staffs for the peak and pays for the quiet hours anyway. The model's bill just follows the calls.

The upgrade cycle is what I keep coming back to. Grok Voice 2.0 shipped July 29. Version 3.0 shipped 11 weeks later at the exact same price, and its score on a benchmark built from simulated support calls jumped from 56.5% to 71.6%. Anyone running on the latest version got switched over automatically with zero code changes. A human center spends $1,000 to $2,000 training each new agent, one at a time. This whole workforce got better overnight.

Around 1.9 million Filipinos work in that outsourcing industry. It brought in over $40 billion last year, roughly 8% of the country's GDP, and for a generation its core pitch has been the lowest price anywhere for a fluent English voice on a phone line.

That voice now costs 8 cents a minute, and on Wednesday it got better without getting more expensive.

note_tweet.text:
interpretability might be the most important scientific problem in the world right now, as I don't think we can solve alignment if we don't know what we're building. I think I have good news about it. I co-authored early work in mechanistic interpretability at OpenAI and came away pessimistic, because neural networks appeared to fold into arbitrary tangled knots. years later, I started openai's first large-scale automated interpretability project, finding about 2% of neurons legible with the primitive tools we had

with modern agentic tools and a much closer look, the picture looks totally different. the vast majority in models up to trillions of parameters are legible, and their circuits beautiful. many famous examples of tangled neurons turned out to be misunderstood. The roadblocks I expected mostly aren't there. I now think ambitious interpretability will be solved by the time we need it most, and possibly quite soon, as automated scientists keep improving. it may be a bitter lesson for interpretability: the simple thing, at absurd scale, works

https://t.co/zHij5zwKGT
